title: Wave Equation
body:
$$
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}
$$

Vibration. $u(x,t)$ is the displacement of a string at position $x$ and time $t$, and $c$ is the
propagation speed. It is Newton's second law for a taut string: acceleration is proportional to
curvature, because curvature is what makes the tensions at the two ends of a small segment fail to
cancel.

One time derivative in the [[Heat Equation]] became two here, and that single change reverses
everything: waves **propagate** rather than diffuse, energy is conserved rather than dissipated, and
the equation runs backwards in time perfectly well.

## d'Alembert's solution

$$
u(x,t) = F(x - ct) + G(x + ct)
$$

Any right-moving shape plus any left-moving shape, at speed $c$. This is the one PDE in the course
with a general solution written in arbitrary functions, and it makes the propagation reading exact:
initial data travels along the lines $x \pm ct = \text{constant}$ (the characteristics) without
changing shape.

On a bounded string, separation of variables gives standing waves
$\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(n\pi ct/L)$: the modes are the harmonics, $n = 1$ is the fundamental, and the
[[Fourier Series]] coefficients of the initial pluck are how loud each harmonic is. **That is the
physical meaning of a Fourier expansion**, and it is why the two courses belong next to each other.
